outcomes.text: Explain that a hypothesis can only be tested by collecting and analysing suitable data.
Name constraints on an investigation: time, cost, ethics, confidentiality and convenience.
Plan ways to reduce problems in an enquiry, such as unclear populations or non-response.
Use terms for data types: raw, quantitative, qualitative, categorical, ordinal, discrete, continuous, grouped, bivariate and multivariate.
Explain the effects of merging categories or grouping numbers into class intervals.
Tell explanatory variables from response variables and place them on scatter diagram axes.
Compare primary and secondary data and judge their reliability and accuracy.
Distinguish population, sample frame and sample.
Explain that 'population' has different meanings in different contexts.
Explain why judgement or convenience sampling is used and the bias risks.
Choose sampling techniques to avoid bias, comparing random, systematic and quota sampling.
Describe a simple random sample and select one using dice, cards, random numbers or calculators.
Use stratified sampling, including calculating strata sizes.
Name data sources such as experiments, simulations, questionnaires and censuses, and acknowledge secondary data.
Explain reliability and validity of collected data.
Identify causes of bias, including sensitive questions, and reduce distortion.
Plan data collection: question design, leading questions, interview types and pilots.
Deal with missing, incorrectly formatted or incomplete responses.
Clean data before processing, including outliers and spreadsheet issues.
Identify and control extraneous variables, including using matched pairs.
Draw and interpret tables, tally charts, pictograms, pie charts, stem and leaf and Venn diagrams.
Interpret population pyramids and choropleth maps, including area and frequency links.
Draw and interpret bar charts, line graphs, time series, scatter diagrams, frequency polygons, cumulative frequency graphs, histograms and box plots.
Calculate frequency density and use it to draw histograms with unequal class widths.
Justify a format for presenting data and produce accurate visualisations, using software wisely.
Spot misleading graphs: bad scales, truncated axes, distorted sizes and 3D.
Compare data sets shown in different formats and present the same data in several forms.
Choose a representation that suits the type of data.
Find skewness by inspection, and by calculation at Higher tier.
Interpret what a skewed distribution says about the spread of values.
Calculate mode, median and mean for discrete and grouped data and see how changes affect them.
Justify which average suits a given context.
Compare data sets using modal class, median and mean.
Calculate range, quartiles, interquartile range, percentiles and, at Higher tier, standard deviation.
Identify outliers by inspection and, at Higher tier, by calculation.
Comment on outliers in light of the original data.
Compare data sets using range, interquartile range and percentiles.
Pair a suitable average with a suitable spread measure to compare samples and populations.
Use means and standard deviations to standardise and compare values.

subtopics.title: Index numbers and rates of change

outcomes.text: Use index numbers such as RPI, CPI and GDP, including weighted and chain-based indices at Higher tier.
Interpret and calculate rates of change over time, such as birth rates, using given formulae.
Use correlation vocabulary: positive, negative, zero, causation, association, interpolation and extrapolation.
Describe correlation strength from a scatter diagram.
Explain that correlation does not imply causation and spot spurious correlation.
Draw a line of best fit through the mean point and use it, with regression at Higher tier.
Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient.
Interpret a Spearman's coefficient on its -1 to +1 scale.
Interpret a Pearson product moment correlation coefficient.
Explain the difference between Spearman's and Pearson's coefficients.
Find trends in time series by inspection and by moving averages.
Interpret seasonal and cyclic patterns and use them to make predictions.
Explain that sample means vary less than individual values.
Use action and warning lines on control charts in quality assurance sampling.
Use sample statistics to estimate population means and proportions.
Use the Petersen capture-recapture formula to estimate a population size.
Explain that larger samples make results more reliable.
Estimate probabilities from collected data using relative frequency.
Compare outcome likelihoods on a 0-1 scale using likelihood language.
Use probabilities to work out expected frequencies.
Work out and interpret absolute and relative risk.
Compare experimental results with theory to spot possible bias.
Explain that experimental probability approaches theoretical as trials increase.
Comment on differences between experimental and theoretical values in terms of bias.
Use two-way tables, sample space, tree and Venn diagrams and addition laws for up to three events.
Use the multiplication law for independent events.
Use conditional probability notation and formula.
Describe and use the binomial distribution, including its mean np.
Describe the normal distribution as symmetrical and bell-shaped.
Use the 68%, 95% and three standard deviation rules for normal data.
